new_statements.quote: Tones Ibanị has a relatively restricted tone-system, distinguishing High, Low and Downstep, like many Ịjọ and Igbo lects. The conventions are as follows; low tone, unmarked ´ high tone ¯ downstepped high tone
new_statements.citation: Blench, Roger (ed.). 2005. A Dictionary of Ịbanị, an Ijoid Language of the Niger Delta. Circulation draft, Cambridge: Mallam Dendo, 25 April 2005 (original ms. by Eldred I. Ibibiem T. Green from mss. by Abe Brown and Adadonye Fọmbọ; typed and edited by Kay Williamson).
new_statements.locator: Front matter, section 'Ibanị phonology and orthography', sub-section 'Tones', p. x (PDF page 11 of 103); phonology section begins p. viii
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (103 pp., Acrobat text layer, 'Microsoft Word - Ibani composite.doc', author Roger Blench, created 2005-04-25). extracted text of PDF page 11 (printed p. x) ends with the passage exactly as quoted: 'Tones / Ibanị has a relatively restricted tone-system, distinguishing High, Low and Downstep, like many Ịjọ and Igbo lects. The conventions are as follows; / low tone, unmarked / ´ high tone / ¯ downstepped high tone'. It sits in the editor's front-matter essay 'Notes on the Ibanị language' (signed Roger Blench), sub-section 'Ibanị phonology and orthography' (starts printed p. viii, PDF p. 9), which opens 'The principal description of Ibanị is in Fọmbọ (1975) a locally-published pedagogic…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ibani is described as a tone language with a small inventory of High, Low and downstepped High; every dictionary headword carries lexical tone (low unmarked, acute high, macron downstep), and syllabic nasals bear tone. The source says nothing about word stress or accent at all; there is no statement of stress position, of stress being absent, or of any interaction between tone and prominence.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. The editor notes (p. i) that a full explanation of the phonology and orthography is still to be reconstructed from existing publications, and (p. viii) that the phonology is very similar to most Ijoid languages; the section is the editor's summary drawing on Fọmbọ 1975.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical/word-level tone on dictionary citation forms; no phrase-level or intonational information.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source describes Ịbanị (Bonny) proper, glottocode iban1261, from material collected at Finima-Bonny (Abe Brown ms.) and Fọmbọ 1975; it is the PHOIBLE source for Ibani. Wikipedia and Ethnologue treat Ibani as a dialect of Kalabari, but the Kalabari phonological literature (Harry 2003 JIPA; Harry 2004 CSLI) describes Kalabari proper (kala1381), not Ibani, and was not used here.

sources.locator: Front matter, section 'Ibanị phonology and orthography', sub-section 'Tones', p. x (PDF page 11 of 103); phonology section begins p. viii
sources.note: Front matter 'Ibanị phonology and orthography' (pp. viii-x): nine vowels with ATR harmony, consonant table, syllabic nasals bearing tone; 'Tones' section p. x: 'Ibanị has a relatively restricted tone-system, distinguishing High, Low and Downstep, like many Ịjọ and Igbo lects.' Low unmarked, acute = high, macron = downstepped high. No mention of stress or accent anywhere in the 103 pages (grep for stress/accent/pitch: none).

sources.note: Transcription note p. 1 only: 'IPA except that c=IPA [tʃ], j=IPA [dʒ], y= IPA [j]; tilde below instead of on top. Low tone unmarked.' No stress or accent remarks in the whole file (grep: none).

sources.citation: Blench, Roger (ed.). 2008. Kalabari dictionary (anonymous 1960s/70s typescript ex Kay Williamson, photocopied by Silvia Kouwenberg). Sister language Kalabari (kala1381).
sources.note: One-page preface only, then a scanned typescript with unusable scanned; nothing on tone or stress. Kept for the record; not an Ibani source.

sources.citation: PHOIBLE inventory 891 'Ibani' (contributors Moran, McCloy, Wright), source key iby_blench2005 = Blench 2005 'A Dictionary of Ibani, an Ijoid Language of the Niger Delta'.
sources.note: Inventory lists 38 segments including two tones (˦ high, ˨ low); no stress information. Confirms Blench 2005 as the only phonological source PHOIBLE found for Ibani.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.1 languoid page iban1261 (Ibani) and its 6 descriptive references (Horton 1962; Köler 1843, 1848; Benamaisia 1997; Ibiama 1989; a mis-attached Gabelentz & Loebe 1843 Gothic glossary).
sources.note: No phonology or tone/stress source listed; classification refs Jenewari 1989 and Connell et al. 2012; status threatened.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Ibani language' (redirects to the Kalabari language article, which treats Ibani as one of three Kalabari dialects) and 'Kalabari language'.
sources.note: Consonant and vowel charts for Ibani and an alphabet; explicitly nothing on tone or stress. References Ngulube 2011a 'Ibani orthography' (NERDC Manual IX, pp. 69-88; ResearchGate 280579938), Harry 2003 JIPA Kalabari illustration, an Endangered Language Fund 2006 project.
